newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers pressure Air Force on pilot's discharge.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers pressure Air Force on pilot's discharge.

text.p: U.S. lawmakers pressured the Air Force on Wednesday to grant the first woman B-52 bomber pilot an honourable discharge rather than court-martialing her on charges including adultery.
The Air Force was weighing Lt. Kelly Flinn's demand that she receive an honourable discharge upon her resignation.

"Lt. Flinn's (resignation request) was forwarded through the chain of command and has reached the secretary of the Air Force for consideration. We do not expect an announcement today," the Air Force said in a brief statement.
Several congresswomen at a Washington news conference called on the Air Force to drop the charges against Flinn.
"Allow her to leave the military with dignity," said Representative Nita Lowey, a New York Democrat, echoing similar comments made on Tuesday by Senate Majority leader Trent Lott.

"Kelly Flinn is not innocent -- but neither is the Air Force," Lowey said. "This case has been bungled from the very beginning. The Air Force should have offered Kelly Flinn counselling, warnings, and a transfer. Instead it has thrown the book at her, treating her like a criminal."

Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall had no comment on the Flinn case after testifying before a Senate Appropriations subcommittee, which was discussing next year's Air Force budget. The Air Force delayed Flinn's court-martial while Widnall considers her resignation.

Widnall could offer Flinn an honourable, general or dishonourable discharge, or she could reject the request entirely. Flinn said she will only accept an honourable discharge, and will take her chances with a court-martial if she is offered anything less.
Unnamed Pentagon officials said on Monday that Flinn was unlikely to receive an honourable discharge, but that was before political leaders began weighing in on the issue.
During Wednesday's hearing, Iowa Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin attacked the Air Force, accusing officials of wasting money chasing down cases of adultery.
"I think the Air Force is looking ridiculous on this," Harkin said. He suggested he might try to add a provision to the Air Force annual spending bill to address the issue.
The senator's comments brought a heated retort from Gen. Ronald Fogleman, Air Force chief of staff.
"It makes us look ridiculous because people don't know the facts," Fogleman said. "What we are doing in the Air Force is not trying to regulate the sexual mores of America."
He asserted the issue was not one of adultery, but of an officer entrusted to fly planes carrying nuclear weapons who had misled superiors and disobeyed orders.

Flinn's civilian attorney, Frank Spinner, commented to reporters about a letter from Gayla Zigo -- the former wife of Flinn's ex-lover Marc Zigo -- that depicted Flinn as a selfish homewrecker. The letter was sent to Widnall and obtained by reporters.

"Less than a week after we arrived to the base, Lt. Flinn was in bed with my husband having sex," Gayla Zigo wrote. "Lt. Flinn did not care about my feelings. She was just out for herself ... Lt. Flinn knew we were married and not separated, but that did not stop her."
Zigo himself spoke publicly on Tuesday, challenging Flinn's claim that she thought he was separated from Gayla when she slept with him.

Journalists caught their first glimpse of Zigo after he emerged from an interview with Spinner. Brown-haired and boyish-looking, he grinned and waved briefly at reporters before being whisked away by Air Force handlers.
Maj. Joe LaMarca, an Air Force spokesman in Minot, declined to comment on how long the court-martial would be delayed. But it was clear Flinn's resignation bid was on the fast track.
It took one day for the request to make its way through the chain of command to Widnall's office, instead of the standard three to four months.
